summary: Defines four new DHCPv6 options that carry configuration information for Kerberos. It gives clients a standard way to learn Kerberos settings when they get their network configuration. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: When a new computer joins a network, it gets settings from a helper. This memo adds four notes the helper can hand over about the network's login system.

questions: how to configure kerberos via dhcp
what are the kerberos options for dhcpv6
how does a client find a kerberos kdc with dhcpv6
subtitle: Four DHCPv6 options that tell a client which Kerberos realm and key servers to use.

tldr.problem: A Kerberos client needs a realm name and the address of a Key Distribution Center, but some networks, such as industrial systems, do not use DNS, which is the standard way to find a KDC.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6784 defines four DHCPv6 options (option codes 75 to 78) that carry a principal name, a realm name, a default realm name and KDC details such as priority, weight, transport, port and IPv6 address.
tldr.outcome: A client can get Kerberos settings from its DHCPv6 server without DNS. Where DNS is also available, DNS information SHOULD be preferred when no other criteria apply.

today: RFC 6784 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2012, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Finding Kerberos Without DNS
sections.content:
In Kerberos Version 5 (RFC 4120), each organization runs a realm, and at least one Key Distribution Center (KDC) is needed. A client must know at least one KDC IP address before it can get a credential and prove who it is to an application server.

RFC 4120 defines DNS SRV records (RFC 2782) for finding a KDC. Some systems, such as industrial ones, do not use DNS, and adding a DNS server may reduce reliability and raise management cost. Many of those systems do use DHCP. For DHCPv4 in PacketCable, RFC 3634 already defined a KDC address sub-option, but a mechanism with a realm name and an IPv6 address that does not depend on another architecture was still missing.

This document fills that gap. It does not replace or modify existing ways to get this information.
sections.eli5: Usually a computer looks up the login server in a phone book (DNS). Some networks have no phone book, so the helper that hands out network settings tells the computer directly.

sections.title: The Four Options
sections.content:
Four options are defined, all with a 16-bit option code and a 16-bit option-len. Except for the KDC option, none may appear more than once in a DHCPv6 message.

  • Kerberos Principal Name (OPTION_KRB_PRINCIPAL_NAME, 75): sent by the client; the server MAY use it to choose configuration parameters. The name MUST follow PrincipalName in Section 5.2.2 of RFC 4120.
  • Kerberos Realm Name (OPTION_KRB_REALM_NAME, 76): the realm the client wants to access.
  • Kerberos Default Realm Name (OPTION_KRB_DEFAULT_REALM_NAME, 77): used by a server to give the default realm to clients and application servers. Its format is the same as the Realm Name option.
  • Kerberos KDC (OPTION_KRB_KDC, 78): configuration information about one KDC.

Realm names MUST follow the definition of Realm in Section 5.2.2 of RFC 4120.
sections.eli5: There are four kinds of notes: who I am, which login area I want, the default login area, and where the login server is.

sections.title: The KDC Option Fields
sections.content:
The KDC option carries Priority and Weight (16 bits each), a Transport Type (8 bits), a Port Number (16 bits), the KDC IPv6 address (128 bits) and a variable-length realm name for which the KDC serves. The option-len is 23 plus the length of the realm name in octets.

Priority and Weight are hints for choosing a KDC, and their use MUST follow DNS SRV (RFC 2782). Transport Type says whether to use UDP (1), TCP (2) or TLS (3); 0 and 255 are reserved and 4 to 254 are unassigned. TCP exchanges are described in RFC 5021, and Kerberos over TLS in RFC 6251.
sections.eli5: The KDC note says where the login server lives, how to talk to it, which door number to knock on, and which server to try first if there are several.

sections.title: Client and Server Operation
sections.content:
The text assumes the client is already configured with a principal name. If the client needs a realm name, it sends a DHCPv6 Option Request Option (ORO) naming the Default Realm Name option, and the server answers with a Reply containing that option.

If the client needs KDC settings, it sends an ORO naming the KDC option. It MAY also include a Principal Name option and a Realm Name option. The server replies with one or more sets of KDC parameters and MAY use the principal or realm to select among them. When more than one set is returned, the client MUST use Priority and Weight as DNS SRV specifies.

If a client supports both DNS discovery and this DHCP method, local policy decides, usually set by the realm administrator before installation. With no criteria given, DNS information SHOULD be preferred. An appendix gives an informative decision flow for such a client.
sections.eli5: The computer asks the helper, 'Which login area is default?' or 'Where is the login server?' and the helper answers with the right notes.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA assigned four option codes in the DHCPv6 Option Codes registry: 75 OPTION_KRB_PRINCIPAL_NAME, 76 OPTION_KRB_REALM_NAME, 77 OPTION_KRB_DEFAULT_REALM_NAME and 78 OPTION_KRB_KDC.

IANA also created the Kerberos Message Transport Types sub-registry under the Kerberos Parameters registry, with initial entries as in the KDC option. Future entries are assigned by the IETF Review policy of BCP 26 (RFC 5226).
sections.eli5: IANA is the librarian who keeps the official list of numbers. It gave these four notes the numbers 75, 76, 77 and 78.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 3315 apply. DHCPv6 messages can be modified in transit, so an attacker who alters or injects a reply could lead a client to a malicious KDC. The RFC treats this as a denial-of-service attack, because a malicious KDC does not know the shared key and cannot go further, and a client holding the shared key can detect it.

A shared, unconfigured workstation may lack a host or service key and so cannot validate the Ticket-Granting Ticket. It would not notice a malicious KDC, which could allow access by unauthorized users.

To reduce the risk, a client SHOULD use DHCPv6 authentication from Section 21 of RFC 3315. Manual configuration of Kerberos information SHOULD be preferred to configuration through the DHCPv6 server.
sections.eli5: If a trickster slips the computer a fake note, it could be sent to a fake login desk. Using a secret handshake with the helper, or setting things up by hand, is safer.

fields.name: Option Length
fields.desc: 23 plus the length of the realm name in octets.

fields.name: Priority
fields.desc: Hint for KDC selection, as in DNS SRV.

fields.name: Weight
fields.desc: Hint for KDC selection, as in DNS SRV.

fields.name: Port Number
fields.desc: Port on which the KDC listens.
